analysis.one_liner: Lets workers earn up to seven paid sick days a year, with smaller employers only required to offer unpaid days.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or any action after being sent to three House committees, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require employers with 15 or more workers to let employees earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours (about seven workdays) a year, to use for their own illness, medical care, caring for family, or dealing with domestic violence or stalking. Businesses with fewer than 15 employees could instead provide 56 hours of unpaid sick time. Workers could not be punished for using the time, and employers with existing paid-leave policies that already meet the standard would not have to change anything.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of workers who currently get no paid sick leave, particularly lower-wage workers in service, retail, and care jobs, would gain the ability to stay home when sick or care for a sick child without losing pay. Workers facing domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking could use the time to seek medical care, relocate, or go to court. Workers without health insurance are protected in the certification process, and the bill builds in a GAO study of who actually gains access, broken down by race, ethnicity, gender, and occupation.

how_it_helps.text: Employees would earn at least 1 hour of paid sick time per 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours a year, usable for their own illness or medical care, to care for a child, parent, spouse, or domestic partner, or for needs arising from domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.
Paid sick time must be compensated at no less than the greater of the employee's regular rate, the federal minimum wage, or the applicable state or local minimum wage.
Employers may not fire or retaliate against a worker for using sick time, count it against a no-fault attendance policy, or require the worker to find a replacement as a condition of taking it.

The bill lets workers sue or file complaints with the Labor Department to recover lost wages, interest, and liquidated damages, plus attorney's fees, and gives the Secretary of Labor investigative and enforcement authority like that under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

Employers who already offer paid leave sufficient for the same purposes under the same conditions would not have to provide anything additional, so the bill mainly targets employers with no comparable policy.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more workers who do not currently offer paid sick leave would bear the cost of paying wages for sick days, plus recordkeeping and notice requirements. Employers with fewer than 15 employees would face a lighter obligation: they could choose to pay, or provide 56 hours of unpaid sick time per year instead. Some businesses would pass costs to customers or limit other benefits; small firms with tight margins would feel the squeeze most.

drawbacks.text: The mandate raises labor costs for employers that do not already offer paid sick leave, and businesses with narrow margins may offset it by reducing hours, slowing hiring, or raising prices, which falls partly on consumers.

Businesses with fewer than 15 employees can meet the requirement with unpaid sick time only, so the lowest-wage workers at the smallest firms would get the right to stay home but not the pay that makes it usable.

The benefit is capped at 56 hours a year, does not carry over beyond that cap, and unused time does not have to be paid out when a worker leaves the job, so it is a modest floor rather than a generous benefit.
Employers may require a health care provider's certification for absences longer than three consecutive days, which can be a real barrier for workers who lack insurance or easy access to a doctor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers without paid sick leave, the benefit is concrete: the ability to see a doctor or care for a sick child without losing a day's pay, which studies and the bill's own design tie to better health and less spread of illness in workplaces and schools. The costs are real but modest by design: a cap of about seven days a year, a 15-employee threshold that lets the smallest firms provide unpaid time, and a carve-out for employers that already meet the standard. The main honest objection is the cost burden on small and low-margin employers, which the bill softens but does not eliminate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced, and no committee ever took it up, so it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Healthy Families Act on May 17, 2023, with 73 original cosponsors.
On the day of introduction, the bill was referred to the Committees on Education and the Workforce, House Administration, and Oversight and Accountability.
The action history shows no further action after the referral: no hearings, no markups, no committee vote, and no floor action.
The bill had 134 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and none of the three committees or House leadership scheduled it for consideration before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who do not currently provide paid sick leave are better off, since they continue to avoid the mandate and its wage costs. Workers who lack paid sick time are no better off than before; the bill left them with nothing.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro

sides.party_line_note: All 134 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill received no action in the Republican-controlled House before the Congress ended.

industries.industry: Employers without paid sick leave (concentrated in service, retail, hospitality, and care work)
industries.note: The bill would force employers with 15 or more workers to pay wages for up to seven sick days a year for workers who now earn nothing when they stay home. The industry's interest in the bill runs against workers' interest in paid time off.

These employers could satisfy the bill with 56 hours of unpaid sick time instead of paid time, avoiding direct wage costs but still losing flexibility when a worker takes leave. Their workers would get the right to take the time but not the pay.

industries.industry: Employers with existing generous paid-leave policies
industries.note: The bill explicitly does not require any additional leave from employers whose existing paid leave already meets its purposes and conditions, so their current position is locked in rather than disrupted.
Workers without sick leave would gain a paid benefit; the bill also preserves any more generous state, local, or collective bargaining provisions rather than preempting them.
